_source: docs/content-bible.md §4 (Ancient lore surfaces), §6 (towns + aging arcs), §7 (gym leaders), §8 (story spine), §9 (side quests), §10 (NPCs), §13.13 (dialogue budget) + build-doc §15 C7. Names of species, places, people and organisations are transcribed from the bible, never invented (G2); the coined quest-NPC given names are logged in docs/DIALOGUE-NOTES.md.
_guardrail: G7 — no moralizing copy about catching, anywhere. NPCs state facts, express their own livelihood interests, and disagree with each other. No line tells the player they did wrong, implies guilt, or delivers a lesson. Enforced by the pattern scan in tests/unit/dialogue.test.ts AND by a line-by-line human-style read documented in docs/DIALOGUE-NOTES.md — a regex cannot detect tone.
_budget: bible §13.13: ~10 lines per named NPC, ~3 per ambient, roughly 400–500 total. Shipped: see _counts. Named speakers that carry an Ancient lore chain or a six-act arc (Maren, Wick, Sel, Bram) run above 10; ambient speakers in the vertical-slice towns run above 3 because they carry year/population state variants the flat budget did not price in.
_conditionModel: An entry fires when every clause of `when` holds. TWO INDEPENDENT CLOCKS (Q3, the authorised L8 amendment): act/actMin/actMax are the STORY clock and every story beat gates on them, so it fires whenever the player earns it, in any calendar year; years/yearMin/yearMax are the WORLD clock — unbounded, never waiting for the player — and only world-ageing copy reads it. THE ACT LADDER IS core/acts.ts actOf(), which is the repo's only act authority and reads data/balance.json acts.gates: acts run 0..6, and ACT 0 IS THE PROLOGUE — a real state every new save starts in, which act 1 opens on story.opening.done. An `act` EQUALITY closes the entry the moment the act advances, so it is used only where the beat belongs to that act and nowhere else (the prologue; each act's arrival greeting); anything a player can walk past and come back to uses actMin, because town N's gym and route N unlock in the same act. seasons gate the four migrant windows; flagsSet/flagsUnset/flagEquals read SaveFile.questFlags; population/floraStock read the LIVE node state (SaveFile.nodeStates), so a town's lines change as its web does — a line that quotes a count or an abundance must carry the clause that makes it true. Among the entries that match a (speaker,node,kind) request the game takes the highest `priority` (default 0). Every greeting/ambient group ships an unconditional fallback, so a matching entry always exists.

_chains.vellsire-chain: bible §4 'Maren's keystone lectures' + 'Duskhollow astronomers on the Vellsire's vanishing'. Steps 1..11 alternate NPC and antler-standing-stone props across Hearthollow → r1 → Brackwater → r2 → r3 → Bowerdeep → Cindershelf → Duskhollow (Orrin) → sanctum-approach → sanctum. Each step is gated on the previous step's flag, so the lore opens as it is earned rather than arriving as one block.
_chains.undermere-chain: bible §4 "Sel's serpent tales". Steps 1..7 alternate Sel and the sunken idols at brackwater/r2; step 5 additionally requires the Ferryman's Wager (bible §9) to be finished. Completing it sets chain.undermere.complete, the gate on the Undermere hunt.
_chains.kilnback-chain: bible §4 'Bram and the miners on the warm shell below'. Steps 1..6 alternate Bram, the miner Gerta and the shell-kiln shrines in the Cindershelf mine. Completing it sets chain.kilnback.complete, the gate on the Kilnback hunt.

lines.text: Right. You came up here after work and there's work going, so you're taken on. The pay is poor and the walking is most of it. There's more ground here than one person gets round in a season.
My name's Maren. Warden for the region, which sounds grander than it is.
There was a keystone animal here once. The Vellsire, a stag. The last of that herd went out of Fallowmere about thirty years back, and nothing out there now does what they did for the ground.
Three in the pen behind you: a Cindril, a Puddlisk and a Thornlet, all in this spring. A young one has about three years of work in it. After that it comes back here and lives on without working.
Have a proper look at all three, because I can't swap it over afterwards.
The Cindril, then. Fire animal, and the quickest of the three by a long way.
It'll be a Vulkindle at two and a Pyrevane at three. Same animal the whole way through with a new name on it each time. Bring it down when it changes and I'll weigh it.
The Puddlisk, then. Water animal.

The skin's clear enough to watch its dinner go down inside it. Rillisk at two, Maelstrisk at three, and they go over in the night, so you come down to something bigger with a different name on the card.
The Thornlet, then. Plant animal, and it'll open your forearm up if you carry it against your chest, so use the crook of your arm. Bramblore at two, Thornwald at three.
Same animal each time, only bigger. By the third year you'll not lift it.
Snares first. Three of them in the satchel by the door, and they're yours to keep. The satchel isn't. One snare holds one animal long enough for you to get your hands on it.
After that there's one fewer where you took it from. Bait makes a snare likelier to hold, and you make it out of whatever the animal eats. A base one lets go of anything that fights hard.
A weighted one holds. A master snare costs more than this station sees in a year.
And this is the survey board. Every place in the region down one side, what's living in it written against the place, and a number against that.
Most of it's mine, and there's only the one of me.
So read it on your way out the north gate and again coming back. Take four of the Nibbin off Meadow Reach and the board reads four fewer when I write it up that evening.
One more thing before you go far. There'll be tracks out on the Reach, and droppings, and a flattened patch where something's lain up. Read one and you'll know what came past and roughly when.
Some things are only here part of the year. Pollywisp are a spring animal on the Reach, so a card read on one in autumn comes back dormant. And a dull animal reads nothing off a good clear track.
Walk Meadow Reach and write me three cards.
Three cards. A Loamunder, a Nibbin, and one you weren't sure of. I'd put that down as Bramblehog.

Three more than I had for the Reach at the start of the week. People who read sign come round to the same question sooner or later: how a few animals matter far more than their numbers suggest. Come and find me in the mornings.
One more thing about the snares. They work the other way round as well. You can open one and let the animal back out.
Whatever you let out goes into the ground or the water you're standing on.

Not back where you caught it. A release goes on the board the same way a catch does, only the number goes up instead of down. Hetty on the shallows has wanted somebody putting Boglings back since spring, so go and see her.
The green's holding up out on the Reach this year.

I'd put a fair bit of that down to the Loamunder turning the soil as they go, and that's a guess, mind. Maribel keeps the gym at the bottom of the green, and it's the old Nibbin that'll give you trouble.
Odo has the gym out on the east stilts. Three weeks since I was over at Brackmarsh, and it rained every day of it, so what I've got written for that marsh is short of what's in it.
The silk and the timber come off the same trees here. I keep a page for the floor of the Wilds and none at all for what's above it, because I can't climb.
Gerta has the steppe survey and can't walk the whole of it on her own. Put your head in on her before you go up.
Orrin's archive goes back further than anything I keep, and I've been up there every morning this week. Ask him straight out and he'll let you read the margins too.
The gate is standing open. It hasn't been open in my lifetime, and it wasn't me that opened it. I'm meant to be counting crows this morning and I've not written a thing down yet.
You asked what a keystone is.
It's an animal a great many other things turn out to depend on, far more than you'd guess from how few there are. Take one out and everything shifts about after it. Not quickly.

Some go up, some go down, and none of it shows on paper for four seasons. Where the Vellsire herd grazed, the ground came back richer the next year, and three people who didn't know each other wrote that down separately.
You read one of the stones out on the Reach. There are more. Another on the Reach, one on the causeway here, one in the Wilds, one on the steppe, one in the vale, two on the Approach.
Somebody set them where that herd used to pass, and whoever cut them was keeping a tally.
The herd hasn't passed in thirty years and the stones go a long way further back. I'd like to know what the tally was of. Some season I'll sit at the causeway stone and copy the face off.
The felling crews let me at a fresh stump when I ask, and I've had forty-odd off them. You can read a tree's years off a stump: a wide ring is a fat year, a thin one is a poor year.
Every one of those forty reads wide, wide, wide, and then thin to the bark.

The thin starts within a season of the last time anybody wrote down seeing a Vellsire. One stump like that and I'd call it a bad tree. Forty of the same I can't. Whether the two things are connected I don't know, and I'd rather say so than guess.
I've not been up that steppe since the thaw. Anything I tell you about it is Gerta's work.

There's less green up there than on the Reach. A place empties from the bottom up. Green goes first, then whatever lived on the green. Last to go is whatever was at the top, and by then it's had nothing since winter.
Four days in that archive and I've read every margin entry rather than take a total on trust.
Two I can't read at all.

The rest were written by different people on different nights across the thirty years the stag's been gone, and none of them wrote down how they got their figure. There isn't a word in the whole book about the standing stones.
The Sanctum Fallow was shut before those stones were cut. Fallow is a farming word. Ground you've left to rest on purpose.
If the herd went anywhere it went in there.

There'll be no herd left to find, though. One animal at the outside, and an old one. What you do standing in front of it is yours to decide, and it'll be a long while before it shows in anything I can measure.
The animal's out of working years. There's nothing wrong with it. It isn't hurt and it isn't ill, it's come to the end of what it had in it.

Two things can come out of this. Either a young one out of the same stock carrying one or two of the things this one was good at, or an animal you've already got gets stronger in one thing for good, under this one's name in the book.
It'll be down at the station from tomorrow, fed, with the run of the yard and no work at all for the rest of its life. Come and see it whenever you're passing.
The west scarp has carried three big Stonewing every year I've had this job. Gerta walked it five days back and found one.

I can't tell you yet what took them off. If it's gone the usual way, the Cragmar and the Ashvole thinned out first, then the Pyrelisk that feed on the Ashvole, and a bird that size feels it last of all.
Greaves went through the gate about an hour ago. He didn't hurry any part of it, and I've been sat here since.
I'll be up on the rim with the board. There's a morning's work still on it. Go on up.

You'll be Maren's, then. The one she's got walking the Reach for her. I'm Wick, second year with the Cullbrand Company, and this route's on my intake sheet. Company pays by the head and doesn't ask whose.
I'm grade four. Eleven a head.
The bird's a Carricrow, which they laugh at me for at intake. In a bad week my team comes back with nothing and this route still pays.
You were quicker than me the whole way through. Not just at the end. The whole way.
I'll write it up in the returns tonight and it'll say I lost. Find me on the marsh road, I take a room over the net loft.
You had the better of me by less than the returns sheet will make it look, and I'll say so on the sheet. You've walked the whole Reach for her. There's half of this route nobody puts a man on.
Brackwater's whole fishery is priced off the Fenmaw, and has been for sixty years. It's in the intake schedule and I can show you the page.
Down here they call it the season, and they eat off it.
Your timing in the shallows is better than mine.
I went early. I always go early out here. Sel poles the channel crossing at the far end, and if you stand still long enough he'll tell you what's under it.
The marsh is slow ground and I've walked it all year. I had that one before either of us put anything out. They put me up to grade five last month. Two more a head.
First thing. I had the fishery wrong. It's priced off the channel. The buyer took the contract off his shelf and made me read the clause out in front of two other men.

The buyer took the contract off his shelf and made me read the clause out in front of two other men. They put me up to grade six the same week. My buyer list has a name off every house on all three levels, and the council.
I've checked. Maren doesn't pay you, and you're not on anybody's books.
Three years running and you've had me every time. If you were ours I'd move you up two grades in an afternoon.
You're not ours and here you are anyway. I've asked about you in three towns. A woman in the market had you down as the warden's own family and she'd never set eyes on you.
I've had this canopy on my sheet since spring, so I know which branches take a landing and which drop you. You don't yet. Come and find me after dark.
You've walked the steppe. I worked it.

Two seasons on the west scarp with a Cullbrand crew, and I took the bonus. Cullbrand paid out on Cinder Steppe for four years, and there were families in four towns eating off that money. I'd work it again if they put me back on that crew.
The scarp went empty in the fifth year. Grade seven now, and part of that came off the steppe.
Not much left standing on this scarp and you came off it with a team on its feet.
Bram keeps the forge under Cindershelf and does relic work. My first Carricrow aged out two winters back and he set the relic off it into this harness.
I've walked every part of this scarp, so I know where the ground gives out under you. Take the rest of the day. The salvage crew doesn't pack up till dark.
Greaves gave me his whole argument once, in a corridor. The animals out there belong to nobody, somebody is going to take them, and the money off them paid for the vale road and my wages.
I've looked for the answer to that and I haven't got one. I'm grade eight now. If you find it, say it to me first.
I could put in for a transfer tomorrow and they'd sign it inside the week. Two men at intake have asked for the vale already. I'm not going to, though.
I want to beat you. And you argue with me and you're still there when it's over.
Wispurr only come up here in the cold months, and while they're here you don't cross this ground without running into one. All winter I've had on it. You've had an afternoon.
There's a thing up on rollers past the gate stone and I've seen the build sheet. It's rated to carry the weight of a barge.
I'm not going in with him.
I was on the steppe crew for a last draw once, so I know what the column looks like the season after. There's nothing under it. That page hasn't been looked at above me since the payout cleared.

I'm grade nine now, so the office will say I've gone soft. I did the sums anyway. What the Company has that animal valued at, and what's left up here once it's gone. Beat me first, and then go and put it to him yourself.
Six years I've been writing you up in the returns, whichever way it went, and my first year's returns are still in a box at intake. The way up is past the gate stone and Greaves has left it clear.
There's a man posted. He's paid by the day.
Then I'll be here a while longer, and that suits me. I'm in no hurry to be the one who walks in behind Greaves. Come back when your team's slept.
Half this job is invoices.
A barge three days late, a buyer who won't sign till he's seen it, and I pay for the room over the net loft either way. Whatever route they put me on, you'll be walking it.

You will have been told a good deal about the Cullbrand Company and very little of it will have been accurate. My name is Greaves. The Bowerdeep accounts are mine, which is why I am standing in a night market at this hour.

Cullbrand does not log Bowerdeep and never has. Cullbrand buys timber and finished silk from parties who log Bowerdeep, under contracts drafted by people I pay well, and my lawyers regard that distinction as material.

Maren has you counting, I understand. We keep something of the same sort. Ours is called an inventory, it is audited in the spring and again in the autumn by people engaged to find it wrong, and it balances to the individual animal.
She is doing that work with a notebook and no staff.
Cinder Steppe was let to Cullbrand on a six-year contract. The schedule was met in four. The board took the view that finishing ahead of schedule was good management, and against the schedule it was.
Nothing else was being measured. I am told the company store shut in the week the crew were paid off. This town had four years of wages out of that contract and nothing since.
There are men on this street who ate better under that contract than in any year after.
You have been counting for the warden for six years, and she has your figures, and I have no quarrel with the figures. My own people would have arrived at much the same numbers eventually, and later.
That view was put to me in writing and it is minuted.

The animal in that ring belongs to nobody, and the board takes the view that an animal of that size with no owner is an asset this Company is entitled to acquire. You are standing between the ring and the teams on the rim.

The afternoon has gone to somebody who walked up here on foot, and I would like that entered accurately. It will not be. I have forty years of records and not one page about a region after a contract closed.
The animal is behind you and nobody is going to stop you.

The result has been entered and the schedule is not affected by it. Neither is the view I took of you when we first met, which was favourable. Come back up when you are ready. The teams are paid to the end of the week.
Bramblehog and Skir, then Old Nib. Three, and the notice on the door still says four. The first two came out of the yard behind the house.
The Bramblehog was hand-reared, her mother had nothing in her that year, and she comes in low and leans on whatever's in front of her. Old Nib is long past her working years, and she doesn't chase.
Whatever's fighting her comes to her and she stands and takes it on that pelt.
Old Nib will want her feet looked at tonight, and she'll bite me for it. Take your badge.
If you're about at the turn of the year, the whole green goes up in lanterns for the festival. Come and have your supper off us, there's always far too much of it.
Old Nib's still on her feet, so she'll be unbearable in the shed tonight. She won't be handled and she won't come in off the yard.
Meadow Reach has gone thin on Nibbin. Mine are penned and hand-fed, so I've the same ones I had in spring.

Costs a fortune in feed. The Skir come in over my hedge, three and four at a time, and they only do that when the Reach has run short. Then they sit on the gatepost looking hard done by till I wave a bucket at them.
I'm in and out of the shed all morning, so speak up.

One of the Bramblehog's off her food and I can't find a thing wrong with her. The other got into the barley again and went straight for the Loamunder. There's a gap in that hedge wide enough for a cart, which is why nobody's mended it.
Hold on. — There's a boat coming in wrong on the far stilts.
Right. Bogling first. Then Reedrick. Whose boat is that.
We go on the slack. Not before. Twenty minutes yet, maybe more. Sit down. Sel made that bench out of a boat that stopped being a boat. The Fenmaw comes out last. She's had the bottom out of two.
Good fight. — The small ones, now. Bogling, we call them at that size. They eat the same Reedrick the big ones eat, only smaller ones. I've had the same animal in my hands at both sizes.
Your badge is in the tin by the door. Sel doesn't carry change.
No hurry from me. Rest up first. I'm on the water most of the day. Want me before dark, wait at the stilts and I'll come in on the slack.
Brackmarsh has gone quiet on Mirefin. Hold on. The ebb's starting.
The fishery pays less when the marsh is short, so the men on the stilts are on a bad week's money. Hetty walks the shallows and I'm out on the water.
The far bank's moved out since the spring. Not much. A foot, maybe two.

There's more Sporantle in this marsh than anything else and no market for them. Somebody boiled a potful down for a dye once, and what came out of the pot was grey and went straight back in the channel.
Halder wants three Webvern out of the Wilds canopy, full-grown. His buyers are contracted, so his case is real.
I walked those lines myself at the end of summer. Eight in that canopy, and he wants three.
The Webvern on the end goes last, and she will get her toxin into whatever is standing when she comes out. Look over the bench as long as you like.
The old Webvern got her toxin into you. It hardly shows at first.
It builds, and by the sixth exchange it is taking a real piece out of whatever is standing. I carry tonics for it. Take the badge, and I will write it up before morning.
The old Webvern gets her strike in the moment she comes out, however quick your animal is. After that she is on her own speed, but the first one is usually enough.
The Barkhide browse the understory back hard, and where they stop it closes over in two summers. That is why there is light down here.
Halder pins his order on the market board and my figure goes up beside it, with the date on mine.
Ashvole. Cragmar. Stonewing. Pyrelisk. Then the other Ashvole. No. The warm one's second, she comes out after the first.
Six on the bench. Take as long as you want, and take your coat off first.
Last one's a Pyrelisk as well. Older. Off the west vents. Two seasons, that one took.
Most of that bench goes out the moment it gets wet. The Stonewing doesn't. Half wind, that one. Bram's through the back, past the slag heap.
Here. Your badge. He takes relics gone brittle, not cracked.
Bench is still warm and I'm not banking it down yet. My forge is the small one, thirty feet that way. Give the door a good bang, because a soft knock doesn't carry over the work.
Gerta's at the head of the third shaft most days. Colder up there than down here.
Take a coat up. Ground's still warm under the west path, warm since the last flare, and my cellar's warm with it, so I buy salt a week at a time.
The room's dark. It stays dark. Bring a lamp for the walk down.
They go out in the order they wake. Last one's a Duskstalk.
Anything of mine can stop an animal where it stands. No warning, and nothing you did. The woman who had this gym before me left that Duskstalk here.
You got through the Duskstalk. Three have done that before you, and I remember all three. Two still come up in the winter and one owes me for a lamp.
Take the badge. The gate on to the Approach is off the vale road, a mile past the last lamp.
Come back when you like. Come at noon if you want to see the room in daylight. The lamps stay lit up here whatever the hour.
The Duskstalk was here before me and she'll be here after. She doesn't look at me.
The Carricrow came into the vale a few years back and stayed. They go where things have died, and the children up here feed them bread.
Rates are on the post. Same in the rain as in the sun.
Forty-one years on this crossing and I've been late the once. My brother's wedding. He's sixty-eight and he still brings it up in front of the whole boat.
Across, then. Sit in the middle and keep your hands inside the boat.
Crossing, or the crossing and the stories? Same money either way. The stories are free.
The story starts with my pole and you're welcome to measure it. Ten feet, near enough. Anywhere along my crossing it finds bottom at five feet, six feet.
In four places it doesn't. I've looked for a fifth all my life.

The whole ten feet goes down and there's still nothing under the end of it. My grandfather marked those four and I mark the same four, only I shifted one of his a foot east. Two have a stone figure sunk on the rim, and you can make the near one out from the dock at low water.
So you've had a look at the figure off the dock rim. That stone is not marsh stone. I had a mason down one summer and he couldn't place it.

My grandfather called the four places the lake-beneath-the-lake. He meant a second water under ours, and the four are where the two meet. Every other stretch of this channel silts up, and in my lifetime those four have not taken a foot of mud.
You can see the near one from the dock at low water.
Right. You got your Mirefin inside the year, so the rest of the tale's owed you. Barge is due in, so you're having this standing on the dock.

The figure is eyeless. The face is finished everywhere else, mind. Where the eyes should be, there was never anything cut at all. My grandfather said whatever's down there came up the once, in a flood year, and the town felt it through the pilings.
He'd never say what he saw. Mind your feet, they're bringing the plank over.
So you've been out to the second figure, the one out in the reeds. The pair of them now, facing each other across two miles of reed. Whoever cut the one cut the other, near enough.
Draw a line between them and it runs right over the third of my four places. I've had the whole ten feet down there and found nothing, and I don't leave the boat sitting over that place.
Go at slack water, not an hour either side. Take something that can swim.
Here. My grandfather's card, and mine underneath his on the same string. Spare string for a third, and nothing of mine to put on it.
The name on the older card is Undermere. The writing is nothing like my grandfather's.
He told me the card was older than the town. It says the thing down there does not age. I don't know what to do with a sentence like that. He believed it, and he was no fool about this water.
Third place, off the Brackmarsh figure, at slack water. Go on, and be back before the evening barge.
A wager, then, while you're crossing anyway. An Elder Mirefin, out of the channel, back to this dock before the year turns. A big old one, not one of the young out of the shallows.
An old one has one year of work left in it. No more than one.
I say that out loud before anybody takes it. Win and you cross free as long as I'm poling this boat. I'm sixty-six, so do that sum yourself. If it doesn't come off, I keep my fare.
Deep edge of the channel. Not the reed side.
An old one holds station out there and lets the current bring its food down. My grandfather baited for them with a Reedrick, because Reedrick is what they eat.
Fair enough. The offer keeps. If I'm not at the post I'm out on the water.
A big one, and heavy with it. Look at the jaw on that.

Comes of holding station in the channel and taking what comes down. Free crossings from here on, and I'll tell the lad on the second boat as well. There's the rest of the tale owing you, whenever the barge isn't in.

Third piling's soft, fourth's going the same way, and nobody's driving new ones. Pilings come out of the levy, the levy comes off what the boats bring up out of the channel, and they're bringing up next to nothing.
I wrote to the harbourmaster in the spring. He wrote back to agree with me. Six times a day I step over that third one.
New pilings under three and four.
The levy came in over what the board had budgeted and they put the extra into the dock. The deck's level enough to roll a barrel down now, which I did not expect.
Mind your feet that side. Hot scale down there and it goes through a boot sole.
If it's the warm floor you've come about, ask away, only ask me while I'm working. My father put my hand down flat on it when I was seven.
Put your hand flat on the floor. Go on. By the anvil, where the flagstone's worn smooth.

Warm, isn't it. My forge is cold till I light it after noon, so it isn't that. And it isn't a vent. A vent comes up hot for an hour and then it's done with you, and this floor has never come up like that.
The men underground call it the warm shell below. Go up and look at the shrine at the shaft head.
You got up to the shrine, then. Take a candle next time and look along an edge where a plate's chipped. Those plates aren't cut stone. They're shell.
I had a broken piece on this bench a month and never marked it. Ask Gerta for her log.
Right. So you got down to the deep shrine.
Kilnback. The word cut on it, in the old letters. Somebody went into that reach and cut a name into a plate wider across than my doors, a long while before my father's father.
My whole working life on this floor and I still can't tell you what makes it warm.
Go down when the vents are quiet. Take something at home in water or made out of rock, because nothing else will take a fire. Mind the last ladder, third rung's split.
So one of yours has aged out. You'll have the relic on you. What it's for is this: I set it into a collar-piece, plain brass.
Bring it here and come back through the town tomorrow.
The young one that wears it carries a bit of what the old one had. A bit of it. I've had grown men argue with me about how big a bit. Wants a day and a night to cool once it's in.
There you are. Collar's cooled through and the seat's tight.
Get your thumb on the relic and try to shift it. You won't. I've put the old one's name underneath, against the strap, the same as on all of them.
Fifth shaft's open as of this spring.

There's enough coming off the steppe to keep a crew fed while they dig, and Cragmar are grazing the high scarp again. My brother's lad has gone on the new shaft, and my brother's wife has said four words to me all week.
Fourth shaft's boarded up now. It didn't fall in. There's been next to nothing off the steppe these two seasons and somebody in an office signed a paper. I said my piece up at the office.
I said my piece up at the office and they left it open. The third stays open and I'll be in it while I can stand up in it.
One reading a shift, off the wall of the third shaft. Thirty-one years of it now. It was nobody's job.
The shift before mine kept saying the third was warmer than the fourth and I wanted to know if they had it right. Then a few winters went by and it seemed daft to stop.
Bram's sent you up for the log. Here. One reading a shift, all of them mine, off the wall and not out of the air.
Eight over the fourth. Same depth, the two shafts, so the two compare.
The eight has never moved, they tell you. It has. It went to fourteen in two winters out of thirty-one years, four days at a stretch each time, and both followed a summer with no vent flare.
Go down the warm reach before you take the log back. There's a shrine at the bottom, not like the ones at the shaft head, and there's no number on it anywhere.
There's a survey wants doing up on the steppe and I'm below all week. It's a day's work, so tell me no if you haven't got a day.

Five I want numbers on, all up on Cinder Steppe. Ashvole, Cragmar, Pyrelisk, Stonewing, Carricrow. Hurry and you'll put the same Carricrow down in two places, because they won't settle anywhere for long.
And walk the west scarp. How far up the green gets now, against the old cairn.
Start at the west scarp, then the vent line, then the low ground coming back. Same order I walked it, so your figures sit by my old ones. If the vent line's flaring, leave it and come another day.
All right. It was a whole day I was asking for, and that's a lot to ask of somebody who's just walked in. Find me at the third shaft head if you get a day spare.
Carricrow first. They only settle where something's died lately, so when their figure comes in high I stop looking at the birds and look at the other four.

Then I work up from what's growing. Ashvole and Cragmar graze it, Pyrelisk take both, Stonewing take Pyrelisk and nothing else up there. If the green goes off that scarp it comes up through the lot of them in order.
Your five go in beside my old ones tonight, in the back of the log.

Four fields, and one of them lies fallow every year whether I want it that way or not. West field this year. It was the west field two years back and all, which is not how the rotation's meant to run.
Mind the gate on the way through. Lift it and shove it at the same time or it won't come.

The Loamunder work my west field for me. They go through the soil all season and the ground they've been through comes up better than the ground they haven't. I didn't put them there. I don't feed them.
Twenty-four my side of the fence. I counted them walking the field, week before last.
So: leave them alone till harvest, twenty-four still there when I walk it, and I pay you a share of the crop. When the crop comes in, mind. Not before. I've nothing to pay anybody with till then.
Or take them instead. Buyers in Hearthollow are paying coin for one of them today.

choices.text: Twenty-four, and I touch none of them.

lines.text: Good. Twenty-four now, twenty-four at harvest, and the share comes off the crop, not out of my pocket. I'll walk the fence at the turn and see how many are still my side of it.
The Reach has its own Loamunder past the north gate. They're not mine and the arrangement says nothing about them.
Fair enough. Offer stands till harvest, and next year as well if you want it. Tell me either way. There's the west field to settle before the frost.
You've left me the twenty-four standing. Two out there are young ones that weren't there in the spring. Here's your share, and it came out heavier than I quoted you, so take the difference.
West field came in at full weight. It hasn't done that in three years.
Same arrangement next year if you're still walking this way. You leave them alone till the crop's in, and I walk the fence at the turn and see how many are still my side of it.

Under the twenty-four on the fence walk this morning, so there's no share off the crop this year. We set it that way at the start. Some years the field carries them and some years it doesn't. There's tea in the house if you want it.
West field goes fallow another year, then. I'll sow the east heavier and make it up somewhere.
Offer's the same next spring if you want it then. The fence gets walked at the turn either way.
Fishery cut me to half hours two seasons back. Half.
So the mornings are mine and I spend them in the shallows. Hetty, by the way. That board by the door is mine, and the third column's crooked because I ruled it crooked in a hurry.
Here's what I want, and I'll be quick. Four Boglings put back in on the Brackmarsh side.
A Bogling turns into a Mirefin inside a year. Four in the shallows now is four in the channel next year, if all four live. They won't. I ask four because I'd sooner have three than two.
Board by my door is where it goes. Chalk, damp on the third column because the door leaks. Read it in the light or you'll take the Brackmarsh column for the channel one.
Brackmarsh side, in the shallows. Stand in the water, don't lean out of a boat. Go on, before the tide's up over the bank.
Brackmarsh side, not the channel mouth. There's a Fenmaw works that mouth and it'll have a Bogling off you. Then it's four on my board and three in the water.
The buyer pays on the channel. Only the channel. My mornings in the shallows have nothing to do with anybody's wage.

The levy comes off the buyer's price and pays for the pilings and the harbour wall, so a thin year in the channel and the dock doesn't get mended. Sel's your man for the pilings, he's had letters about those.
Mine's four Boglings on the Brackmarsh side.
Four in. Brackmarsh column up by four.
It hasn't moved since I ruled it. I'll chalk it before the damp gets at the board, and the buyer won't see those four for a year.
Silk and thread here, and finished bolt if you want it woven already. Paid on the day, in coin.
Webvern silk takes a dye nothing else in Fallowmere will take, so a bolt goes out at four or five times what the timber fetches. A fifth of that comes to me and it's my whole living.
You're after work? I have work. Three Webvern, full-grown, alive, delivered to the winding house.

Now, the awkward part, and it comes with the terms rather than after them. Vesper has been at the council about this order all season, and her case is that three grown Webvern is more than that canopy puts back in a year. I want the order filled and she wants them left where they are.
We've argued it for years, a fair bit of it in her own kitchen.
My price, paid the day they reach the winding house. Or go and hear Vesper out first, she's at the council table until dark.
Full-grown only. A young one spins a thread you can pull apart.
They hang in the high lines out in Bowerdeep Wilds, above where the loggers are cutting. They are poisonous, all of them, and the lads at the winding house get bitten inside their first month.
Go on, then. She's on the council side of the market until dark and she'll give you her figure down to the last one. Come back either way, because the order stands.
Three, full-grown, and the winding house has them off you already. Here's your money, today, in coin, the way I said. Vesper will have a new figure by the festival.
She always does, and she always reads every line of it out to the council.
The lantern road's mine. Winding house out to the eastern stair, there and back, every night that wants lighting. Kit's in the box by the gate.
Four lamps out past the second bend tonight.
Moths start tonight. Gloomoth, up out of the Wilds, through the town, and on to wherever it is they go.
They put the lamps out as they come through. Not on purpose. There's that many moths in the air at once that a flame won't hold, and every autumn I'm short-handed for it.
So I want somebody walking out to the eastern stair with me and back, one night, with the relight kit, while the moths are still coming through.
Duskstalk work the dark stretches, so we go out together or not at all.

choices.text: I'd rather not walk it in the dark.

lines.text: Stay on the lit stretch, and move when I move. Slow walk out, slow walk back. If a lamp goes out we stop and light it before either of us takes another step.
Right. Then I'll walk it dark. I've done that plenty. Ask me again before the moths are through. After that there's no job left till next autumn.
Every lamp lit, out and back. Good walking. The Duskstalk turned at the stair and never came down the road. They won't come down a lit one.
Put the kit back in the box by the gate, would you. Moths'll be gone by winter, and I'll miss them.
Two censuses in this building. The one overhead is the sky and belongs to everybody. The one on the ground is animals, and it is mine.
The ground one is kept to a written standard, and the standard is nailed up beside the door.

I want a card for every animal you have taken and kept. One card each, by name. The Bogling gets a card and the Mirefin gets a card, because they do not look alike. Orrin calls that fussy. He files by species.
Bring me a name the census has not got and I will have a plate painted for it.
Anything that goes away for part of the year gets that marked on its card. Dormant or migrating, two different words for two different things.
Hold the plate by the edge, the paint is still tacky.

Thirty-five names in the full census and nobody in Fallowmere has all thirty-five written down. I am four short. Three of the four have a single animal apiece, and the fourth came in with no date on it.
Ives has the eyepiece and the ground census, through the arch on the left. I have the shelves. Go through whenever you like.

I am sorry about the light in here. It is not the lamp. The lamp is four years old and burns as well as it did the day I bought it. Ives says the trouble is my eyes. Somebody could still look at the lamp.
The vanishing. Yes. I can read you some of it, if you like.

The sky is logged here every night and has been since the observatory got its roof on. Anything that crosses the vale underneath the instrument goes in the margin of that night's page. A herd, a cart, a man with a dog.

There are two hundred and six margin entries for Vellsire in ninety years of pages. Herds of nine, of twelve, of four, almost all inside the same three weeks of the year. Then one entry in three different hands, all three describing a herd of six crossing toward the caldera.
After that night there is nothing more in the margin. I looked for a falling-off first and there is none to find. Thirty years of nights, and not one Vellsire in any of them.

The book does not have where they went. It only ever held what crossed the vale. The antler stones on the roads were standing long before anybody here kept a book, and somebody was going out and keeping them up for years after.

The stones stand in an order, and the mark on each points at the next along. Meadow Reach, then Brackmarsh, then the Wilds, then the steppe, then the vale, then the Approach. I copied that order out of a surveyor's letter of the sixtieth year.
The marks are cut in, not painted. They are shallow now, and mossed over.
Do not scrape at them. Copy what you can read, and where you cannot, write that down as well. Walk them in that order and bring me what each one says.

choices.text: I'd not get to the sixth this year.

lines.text: In order, if you can. The marks make little sense read out of turn.
The sixth I would leave until last. It is the largest of them and it carries the herd on both faces, so walk round the back of it before you put your pencil away.

No, no. That is quite all right. I am at the shelves most afternoons, and in the evenings when the lamp allows it. The last entry in that book was written thirty years ago, and nothing about it is urgent.
All six, and in order. Thank you. Sit down while I lay them out. Read across, they give a direction and they give a season.
The walk over here is beyond me now.

The direction will not surprise anybody in this vale. It points at the Sanctum Fallow, and people here have said so for years with not one page behind it. Take this to Maren, the direction and the season both, since it will have to be her that comes.
FIELD STATION — HEARTHOLLOW. Survey sheets go up at first light. Pencil and blanks in the tin by the door. Sign for the sheet you take.

In pencil underneath: north gate for the Reach, not the west track, that's been under water since the thaw. Pencil's gone from the tin again. Under that, smaller, in the warden's own hand: yes, and thank you.
FORAGE SIGN — MEADOW REACH. Know four signs: tracks, scrapes, castings, browse line.
MIGRATING: the season either side of this one. DORMANT: further off than that. Neither of those, and no sign on the ground, means the animal has gone.
On the north rise: one block of granite cut into branching antlers, taller than a person, set deep. The turf has grown over the foot.
The weather side is worn round and pale. On the sheltered side, cut shallow, a herd of six figures, with a line running north out of them and off the edge of the stone.
Where the meadow grass banks against the foot, the stone is warm to the hand.
The southern stone is snapped off at about half its height.
The break carries the same lichen as the rest of the stone. What is left of the carving is hooves and the bottom of a line, and the line runs off the broken edge, north, toward the high ground.
A stone figure stands in the water off the dock rim, turned out toward the channel. Only the crown of the head is above water, and the carving there is finished down to the parting in the hair.
The shallows round it are clear to the bottom. The water directly under it is not, and the face does not come clear from the rim.
The dock wall behind it is built of a different stone.

The second figure stands where the reeds thin, in shallower water than the one at the dock. It is turned back to face that one, and the carving is the same, so far as the dock figure can be seen at all.
The eyes on this one were never cut.
Between the two of them the reed stops growing in a band about a boat wide. The water inside the band is darker than the water on either side of it.
The causeway stone leans downhill toward the water.
The peat has banked against the uphill side of it, about as high as a knee. The weather has taken the top of the carving away. Below that, six figures, and a line running east out of them.
The shallower cut runs its full length. The deeper stops before the edge.
NIGHT MARKET — open dusk to dawn. Stalls sell silk, thread, dye, lamp oil, relight kits. The rent falls due the first night of the month, in coin.
Pinned under it on a scrap: the Webvern figure for the town canopy, midsummer. Eleven struck out, nine struck out, seven. Across that in ink, another hand: stop writing on my notice.

The forest has grown up around this stone. It is cut from the same granite as the stones out on the meadow. Two trunks stand hard against its sides, and both trunks have gone flat where they touch it.
There is no granite anywhere in these woods.
Six figures again on the sheltered side, in the same order as the six on the marsh stone. The line runs east out of them and off the edge, level with the flattened place on the nearer trunk.
A low structure at the shaft head, built of curved plates fitted without mortar.
The plates have the colour of fired clay. They are not clay. Up close the grain runs the way bone runs, fired hard enough to come out that colour, and each plate is thicker through than a door.
They have worn hollows into the plate underneath, and every hollow is black with soot.
The second shrine is at the bottom of the deep workings. The air here has not moved in thirty-one years.
The shrine is warmer than the rock it stands on. It has no joins anywhere: a single plate, curving away on both sides, shoulder height, with no tool mark on the outside.

Cut across the face, in a lettering the mine gave up using: KILNBACK. The wax below the letters has built up, been cut back with a knife, and built up again. There is a candle standing in it now, still soft.
Vent heat has glazed the windward face of this stone to a skin of glass, and the glass has crazed and lifted in patches.
The sheltered face has none of that, and the cutting there is sharp. Six figures on it, the line out of them running south-east. Ash lies thick out here, and none of it has caught in the cutting.
Most of this board has been torn away at the tacks. What survives of the printed half reads: PLATES THIS YEAR — NINE.

The rest is later hands on the bare wood. One small: plates go out when the illustrators have time, and asking again does not move you up the list. One slower, signed Orrin: the margin book is no part of the star census.
This stone stands in open ground, with nothing higher than the grass for a quarter mile round it. There is no sheltered side.
The cutting is shallow the whole way round. Six figures again, and the line out of them runs up the face and off the top edge instead of across it.

The gate stone is the largest on the road up, about double the height of the one out in the vale. It is set into cut rock rather than into ground. This stone carries the herd on both faces, and none of the other stones does.
On the outward face the six are walking in. On the inward face they stand still.
A second stone further up the road, left unfinished. The antlers are roughed out to about half their depth, and the face where the herd would go has not been cut at all.
Tools lie at the foot of it under the ash: a hammer and three wedges, side by side. The ash over them takes a boot in to the ankle.
Nine stones at the caldera heart, evenly spaced, every one facing in toward the middle. All of them are carved, and the carving on these is not a herd.
Each stone carries one animal on its own, cut to double the size of the figures on the stones outside. The grass inside the ring is short and even.
It is the only grass in the Sanctum Fallow that anything has been grazing, and the dung lying in it has not dried out.
The stag comes down into the ring from the high side of the caldera. It does not hurry.
It is a Vellsire. The branching on its antlers is the branching cut on every stone from Meadow Reach up to here, and the spread is wider than a person is tall.
It stops in the middle of the ring, on the short grass, and puts its head up. It has not moved off, and it is not looking back at the way it came in.

choices.text: Set the snare. It's the last one.
Leave it. It's the last one.

lines.text: You've got the stag, then. Let me look at it a minute. It's narrower through the shoulder than the drawings have it, and the near antler's been broken and grown back crooked. It won't age.
Right. The numbers, then. Meadow Reach, Brackmarsh, Bowerdeep Wilds, Cinder Steppe, Duskhollow Vale and the Approach, all six walked and counted this morning. Five by me and the steppe by Gerta.

With that animal held, the ground round the Sanctum and along the Approach holds at the rate it has held every year I've walked it: two young brought on, where three is what it makes with the stag loose in there.
I'll write in the book that the snare held and what was in it. Whoever keeps this book after me will want to know why this ground reads as it does.
The stag went up the scarp and over the rim and out of sight. It stopped the once at the top, side on, long enough for me to see all of it. I had a pencil in my hand and never wrote a thing down.
Right. The numbers, then. Meadow Reach, Brackmarsh, Bowerdeep Wilds, Cinder Steppe, Duskhollow Vale and the Approach, all six walked and counted this morning. Five by me and the steppe by Gerta.
With that animal loose, the ground round the Sanctum and along the Approach comes off that rate for the first time: three young brought on, where two is what it has always made.
You were six years getting to it. In nine years somebody will ask me why the numbers moved, and I'd rather they had all of it from me.
Boots are by the fire. They were wringing, so I moved them.
Kettle's on and I'll not be thanked for it. Bed's at the back and your animals will be right by morning. Room only, or supper as well?
The rooms sway. You'll say you won't sleep.
They're built out over the water on the stilts, so they move all night. You'll sleep. The man in the end room said the same and I heard him through the floor by ten.
Your animals come down fit for the evening, and that is in the rate. Four, five, six — linen. Where was I. Day rate, because the night's when the market's open.
I'd sooner have the money now. Take the key off the hook and go up yourself.
Vent side's warmer and it shakes. Other side's cold.
People ask for the quiet side and then move at two in the morning. Your creatures will pick up overnight, and the tubs fill off the hot spring, which costs nobody in this town a thing.
Shutters stay open. Top and bottom, all night, every room. Rule eleven, and it's the observatory's rule, not mine. They made me read all twenty-two out loud.
Third blanket's in the press. You'll be round by daylight, more or less.
Snares and salve. Tonic's on the shelf behind me, and it costs what it costs.

Bait's in the crate by your knee, not sorted, so dig. Cheap sort's cut for a whole kind of animal at once, and it's made of whatever that kind eats. The dear ones are cut for one animal and cost three times the money.
Weighted snares when the smith has iron. None since spring.

The reed bait's the bundle on the end of the trestle, and it has sat there since the thaw. There's nothing out on that marsh will look at it but a Reedrick, and Reedrick only come through in the summer.
Salve, though. Salve moves. Everybody comes off that marsh cut about the hands.
Tonic when I've got it in, and I've none this week.
Night market. Dusk to dawn, and no, we don't do mornings.

Lamp oil, wicks, tonic, silk by the bolt — evening to you! — silk by the bolt. Master snares? Two a year come up here. Well. One. Two sounds better. Come autumn a Gloomoth drops on the rail and everybody steps round it.
It's grazing the moss and hasn't noticed there's a stall here.
No master snares since the contract closed. No tonic either, and none coming.
Base snares, salve, and the cheap bait. There's nothing on this steppe to cut a proper bait out of, so the cheap sort is all there is, and it'll fetch a Cragmar as often as an Ashvole.
My prices went up the month next door boarded its windows.
You'll want the other tin. That one's for the wick.
The fill's in the flat tin at the end. Wispurr bait only moves in the winter, so I buy it in the autumn and sit on it. In summer I'll sell you a tin gone hard, at the same money.
A master snare in the drawer these eighteen months. I don't ask and they don't say, and the observatory buys its oil off the lampwright direct.
You'll be off up the Reach, then. I drove cattle up there. Not this gate. The old gate, down past the mill, and there was never any call to move it that I saw.

Grass does well up there. Always has. Which is — anyway. Skir come over the hedge at dusk hunting Nibbin out of the tussock. I've watched one drop and come up with nothing in it, and go up, and drop again twenty foot along.
Mind the gate on your way through. Have I told you about the gate.
The Reach has come up green right down to the fence line.
Tolm will get a crop off his west side in a year like this. His father had that field in oats. Tolm put it down to grass when he took it on, and he'll have had a reason.
The Reach is short this year. I'd have had the beasts down off that rise a month early.
The town fields go the way the Reach goes. Tolm's west side goes first. It went first the year of the wet harvest and all, and that was before ever he touched the drainage down there.
Maren let me hold the survey book. No drawings in it at all.
There's a Nibbin under the mill step and her name is Kettle. I told Maren her name and she wrote her in as a Nibbin. Just Nibbin.
My da says I'm not to keep on at her. I'm going to keep on.
Kettle's gone white round the face.
She's the same one and I'd know her anywhere. Maren wrote her in again at the turn and the book still just says Nibbin, and I'm learning to write so I can put it in myself.
West gate's down again. Bramblehog, same post. Back up before dark.
Loamunder go along under the west field all night. I've ploughed it top and bottom and never turned one up.
Six weeks to harvest and dry all week. Two hands, four fields.
A track's the easy sign. A browse line takes longer. It's where something's come along and eaten the tips off a bush and left the stems standing, and the bush is still stood there, mind. With me?
The stems are what I measure. A folding rule, notched.

Scrapes now. A scrape is bark rubbed off. Dug is different and dug leaves a cast, and people mix the two up all the time. Pollywisp you'll not see till the spring comes round, because the rest of the year they're down in the wet ground.
Fence line's four miles. I walk it spring and back end and mend what's down.
Cart gets to the second stile and I carry the rest. Something comes through the wire down the west end and takes the post out of the ground with it. Heavy, whatever it is.
Warden wants a number off me. I showed her the post. She wrote something down.
Barge alongside at slack, and slack's an hour off.
She'll not come in on a running tide, not with sixty ton in her. Mirefin out in barrels, flour and nails and rope in, and I've eaten out of every barrel that's crossed this dock.
You try putting sixty ton alongside on a running tide.
I keep off the third piling now when she comes alongside. Sixty ton onto soft timber.
Half the barrels we put out before, so there'll be no new piling driven this year.
Came alongside at slack and the deck never moved under her.
New timber on the third piling and the fourth. First these boards have had in eleven years. My boot still goes down where the soft one used to be.
Coarse mesh for the grown Mirefin, fine for the Bogling. Summer mesh on the end rail for the Reedrick, and that one hangs dry three quarters of the year. I've taken it down a gauge since.
Water's colder than it was when I started, so what comes up comes up smaller.
Colder water. The mesh follows the water, same as it always has.
Sel says don't trail your hand over the side. I trail my hand.
I sit at the front of his boat and take the line off him at the steps. He hasn't said about that.
I've got a boat name now, because I go out in the boats. Corbett hasn't got one and he's been here for ever.
My post is the second one past the steps.
My grandfather cut a mark in it, down at the water line. The water comes up to that mark. Never over it, not in my life.
Drought year, flood year. Same mark. Same mark. The bread's up that way, so I go past it most mornings.
I buy the season here for an office that is not in this town. The schedule comes down in the first week of the year and I price against it.
Clause four says channel. It does not say shallows and it does not say marsh, and it has stood unamended for sixty years.
People bring me marsh figures every spring. Fenmaw take Mirefin, and Mirefin is the animal the contract is written on, so I file the marsh figures and price off the channel.
The warden walked that marsh again last month. She could not put a second Fenmaw in it.
Mirefin come up thick with nothing taking them and then the channel goes empty. There is a clause for that and it sets the price low.
The best week of my year, this. Third year I've come up for the picking.
The grass is four or five days further on than the same week last year, and the tussock's crept north on me as well. A hundred paces from the old edge to the new.
Wet springs, that'll be. There's an antler stone up on the north rise and I have my dinner against it.
I walked the whole tussock this morning and turned up two Nibbin. Two. Last year I'd have seen a dozen before the gate.
The Skir are still about. They're over the far hedge these days, off somebody else's ground.
I've not picked the Reach this thick before. Knee-high on the north rise.
The same week last year it was no higher than my boot. The Nibbin have grazed that rise all week and there's grass standing yet, and the Bramblehog I put up on the path hardly troubled to move.
I take the second boat when Sel's is full, which is most days. People will stand on that bank a quarter hour for his rather than get in with mine.
His boat's no faster. It isn't.
Channel's on your left going out, shallows on your right, and most people never ask. There's an idol out where the reed thins and it faces the town, and I'll point it out on the way if you want.
Reed's gone quiet. Come summer you can't normally hear yourself out here.
Sporantle coming up thick on the mud, thicker than I've ever had them. It goes in the fare book, which nobody has ever asked to see.
I'm my own crew, me. One saw, one man.
My back went two summers ago and I can still put a tree down exactly where I want it. Getting up off the ground after is the trouble, and my wife has heard that one often enough to say it for me.
Below the town the Barkhide eat the low growth back to the dirt, and on ground like that a log walks down to the road one-handed.
There's not a stick left in there worth me walking in for, and I've not had a saw out past the east stair in four years.
No Barkhide on those slopes now, so the low growth has come right up and the young trees under it all came on in one season. The canopy is thinner than when we were cutting under it.
Grown Webvern silk I can tell through a glove. Both hands on a strand, pull as hard as I like, it holds. Young stuff comes apart on the frame while you're winding it.
Second grade. It doesn't leave here as anything else.
People who have never had a hand on it want a number for it.
When the moths come through the lamps go out, poof, poof, poof.

One went down my collar and I had it in both hands and then it got away. The silk comes off the wings. Off the moths. Gloomgrub are the little ones and they're no good for it, you want the big ones out of the high lines.
I'm minding the stall. Got a copper?
Floor stair, was it? They all come up that way. On the walk we would have called that a floor matter, and on the floor they would have sent it up to the walk.
In my day a person knew which.

That was the lampkeeper's family, the ones who sent it up. His father before him, and his father's brother, who married a woman off the canopy, which was not done then and is not much done now. There is a great deal more of it, if you have an afternoon.
First the lower run. Forty-one, forty-two, forty — no. Lost my place. Back down to the first lamp and start again.
Oil's in the shed behind the winding house. — Was it oil you wanted?
Pell has the stair. Mine's the walk, and mine is two hundred and eleven. In the autumn the moths put the lot out and I light two hundred and eleven again.
Warm? Third's warm, aye. Hands know it before I'm off the second ladder. Comes off the vents, that.
Pyrelisk? Up the vent line when it flares. Not every flare, mind. Took the hair off my arm, the once.
Come round this side and say it again. Left ear's no good since the fourth shaft.

Umbrat graze the same ground alongside my sheep, and the Wispurr come up hunting them once the cold's in, and neither has ever had a lamb off me. I go up past the Sanctum gate with the dogs and come back down at dusk.
